Data Visualization with ggplot2 in R

Anil

2026-07-30

Introduction

ggplot2 is an open-source data visualization package in R based on the Grammar of Graphics. Instead of writing long, ad-hoc plotting code, ggplot2 lets us build a plot layer by layer, where each layer has a well-defined job.

Why ggplot2?

  • Based on a layered approach — plots are built up piece by piece.
  • Produces clear, customizable, publication-quality visualizations.
  • Widely used in data analysis, statistics, and data science roles.

The Seven Layers of the Grammar of Graphics

# Layer Purpose
1 Data The dataset being visualized
2 Aesthetics Maps variables to visual properties (x, y, color, …)
3 Geometrics The type of plot (points, lines, bars, …)
4 Facets Splits data into subplots (small multiples)
5 Statistics Transformations — smoothing, binning, summaries
6 Coordinates Controls the plotting plane / axis limits
7 Themes Non-data visuals — fonts, gridlines, legend position

Every ggplot2 call is built by adding (+) these layers together.

Step 1: Install and Load Required Packages

We’ll use the built-in mtcars (Motor Trend Car Road Tests) dataset, which contains fuel consumption and 10 aspects of automobile design and performance for 32 automobiles.

# Run once if not already installed
# install.packages("vctrs")
# install.packages("dplyr")
# install.packages("ggplot2")

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
head(mtcars)
##                    mpg cyl disp  hp drat    wt  qsec vs am gear carb

Identify which columns in mtcars are continuous (e.g. mpg, hp, wt) versus categorical/discrete (e.g. cyl, am, gear) — this distinction matters when choosing aesthetics later.

Step 2: The Data Layer

The data layer defines what dataset feeds the plot. Note that with no aesthetics and no geometry, ggplot2 only draws a blank canvas.

ggplot(data = mtcars) +
  labs(title = "MTCars Data Plot")

Step 3: The Aesthetic Layer (aes)

aes() maps variables in the data to visual properties. Here we map horsepower (hp) to the x-axis, miles per gallon (mpg) to the y-axis, and displacement (disp) to color.

ggplot(data = mtcars, aes(x = hp, y = mpg, col = disp)) +
  labs(title = "MTCars Data Plot")

Notice: the axes are now scaled correctly, but there are still no points on the plot. Aesthetics tell ggplot where things go — a geometry layer is required to tell it what to draw.

Step 4: The Geometric Layer

Geometries (geom_*) control how data is actually displayed: points, lines, histograms, bars, boxplots, etc.

4.1 Basic scatter plot

ggplot(data = mtcars, aes(x = hp, y = mpg, col = disp)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Miles per Gallon vs Horsepower",
       x = "Horsepower",
       y = "Miles per Gallon")

4.2 Adding a size aesthetic

Mapping disp to point size instead of color — larger engines appear as bigger dots.

ggplot(data = mtcars, aes(x = hp, y = mpg, size = disp)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Miles per Gallon vs Horsepower",
       x = "Horsepower",
       y = "Miles per Gallon")

4.3 Adding shape and color categories

Using color for cylinder count (cyl) and shape for transmission type (am) lets us encode two categorical variables in a single plot.

ggplot(data = mtcars, aes(x = hp, y = mpg, col = factor(cyl),
                           shape = factor(am))) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Miles per Gallon vs Horsepower",
       x = "Horsepower",
       y = "Miles per Gallon")

4.4 Histogram

ggplot(data = mtcars, aes(x = hp)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5) +
  labs(title = "Histogram of Horsepower",
       x = "Horsepower",
       y = "Count")

Step 5: The Facet Layer

Facets split the data into subsets and plot each subset as a small multiple, sharing the same axes — useful for comparing across groups.

5.1 Row-wise faceting (facet_grid(rows ~ .))

p <- ggplot(data = mtcars, aes(x = hp, y = mpg, shape = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point()

p + facet_grid(am ~ .) +
  labs(title = "Miles per Gallon vs Horsepower",
       x = "Horsepower",
       y = "Miles per Gallon")

5.2 Column-wise faceting (facet_grid(. ~ cols))

p + facet_grid(. ~ cyl) +
  labs(title = "Miles per Gallon vs Horsepower",
       x = "Horsepower",
       y = "Miles per Gallon")

Tip: facet_wrap(~ variable) is often more convenient than facet_grid() when there is only one faceting variable, especially with many categories.

Step 6: The Statistics Layer

Statistical transformations summarize or model the data — binning, smoothing, descriptive statistics. Here we add a linear regression trend line with stat_smooth().

ggplot(data = mtcars, aes(x = hp, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  stat_smooth(method = lm, col = "red") +
  labs(title = "Miles per Gallon vs Horsepower")
## `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

The shaded gray band represents the confidence interval around the fitted line.

Step 7: The Coordinates Layer

The coordinates layer controls the plotting plane itself — axis limits, scaling, and aspect ratio.

7.1 Custom axis limits and equal coordinates

ggplot(data = mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  stat_smooth(method = lm, col = "red") +
  scale_y_continuous("Miles per Gallon", limits = c(2, 35), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_x_continuous("Weight", limits = c(0, 25), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(title = "Miles per Gallon vs Weight",
       x = "Weight",
       y = "Miles per Gallon")
## `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

7.2 Zooming with coord_cartesian()

Unlike scale_*_continuous(limits = ...), which drops data outside the range, coord_cartesian() zooms in visually without discarding data — important when a smoother is fit over the full dataset.

ggplot(data = mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = hp, col = am)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth() +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(3, 6))
## `geom_smooth()` using method = 'loess' and formula = 'y ~ x'
## Warning: The following aesthetics were dropped during statistical transformation:
## colour.
## ℹ This can happen when ggplot fails to infer the correct grouping structure in
##   the data.
## ℹ Did you forget to specify a `group` aesthetic or to convert a numerical
##   variable into a factor?

Step 8: The Themes Layer

Themes control the non-data ink: grid lines, fonts and text size, and legend position. Common built-in themes include theme_minimal(), theme_classic(), and theme_bw().

ggplot(data = mtcars, aes(x = hp, y = mpg, col = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(title = "Miles per Gallon vs Horsepower",
       x = "Horsepower",
       y = "Miles per Gallon",
       col = "Cylinders") +
  theme_minimal()

try theme_minimal() , theme_classic() and theme_bw() and discuss which best suits a printed report vs. a dashboard.

Putting It All Together

A single plot combining several layers: data, aesthetics, geometry, statistics, and theme.
